sections.sectionSummaryBrief: Moshe is called the faithful shepherd, with two meanings: he nourishes Israel with faith, bringing it from an encompassing state to inwardness, and this extends to his manifestations in every generation.

translations.translation: And to explain this,
the maamar first states
that Moshe Rabbeinu is called "Raaya Meheimna,"
and there are two explanations of this.
That he is a faithful shepherd of Israel, and that he nourishes and sustains Israel in the matter of faith.
For the faith that exists in Israel from their own essence—
that Israel are believers, children of believers—
can be in the category of encompassing (makif),
and this that Moshe shepherds and nourishes Israel in the matter of faith means that the faith should be in inwardness (penimiyus).
And this is what is said in the Zohar,
"That supernal faith will be nourished and sustained from him through you"
(through Moshe),
for this that Moshe nourishes and sustains the faith is that he draws it into inwardness.
And the maamar continues,
that this that Moshe is "Raaya Meheimna"
also refers to the extension of Moshe in every generation,
for the heads of the thousands of Israel in every generation strengthen the faith of Israel
(of their generation),
so that their faith should be in inwardness.
And like Mordechai,
who was the extension of Moshe in his generation,
as our sages said,
"Mordechai in his generation is like Moshe in his generation,"
for even at the time of Haman's decree,
when Torah study and observance of mitzvos were connected with self-sacrifice (mesirus nefesh),
he assembled many congregations to strengthen their faith in Hashem and to stand firm in Torah study and observance of mitzvos.
And after explaining at length that Moshe and his extension in every generation strengthen the faith of Israel,
the maamar explains
the precise wording of the verse, "pure olive oil, beaten for the light"
("for the light" [lamaor] and not "to illuminate" [leha'ir]),
that during the time of exile,
when each person is broken and crushed,
"beaten" (kasis),
through this one reaches the "light" (maor)
(the essence [Atzmus])
from which the light emanates.
And one must understand the connection between this explanation of "beaten for the light" and what was explained
(in the maamar)
previously, that Moshe
[and his extension in every generation]
nourishes and sustains the faith so that it should be in inwardness.

sections.sectionSummaryBrief: The Jews in the time of Achashverosh fulfilled and received what they had begun at Mount Sinai, achieving a higher level through actual self-sacrifice, led by Mordechai.

translations.translation: Now, the explanation of the verse "And you shall command" comes
(in the maamar)
as a continuation of what was explained at the beginning of the maamar,
that the explanation of "And the Jews received what they had begun to do"
is that they received what they had begun at the time of the Giving of the Torah.
For at the Giving of the Torah there was the beginning
("they began to do"),
and in the days of Achashverosh
(at the time of Haman's decree)
there was the receiving,
"and the Jews received."
[And as our sages said
on the verse,
"They fulfilled and received the Jews,"
they fulfilled what they had already received,
for this that they prioritized "we will do" over "we will hear" at the Giving of the Torah was only the receiving,
and in the days of Achashverosh
they fulfilled what they had received.]
And the maamar notes,
that this is seemingly astonishing,
for at the Giving of the Torah Israel were at the peak of elevation,
and there was then a revelation of G-dliness at the most sublime level
[in addition to the fact that even before the Giving of the Torah there were most sublime revelations,
the revelation at the Exodus from Egypt and especially at the Splitting of the Sea,
the revelation at the time of the Giving of the Torah was an even more sublime revelation],
and in the days of Achashverosh Israel were at the peak of descent,
for in addition to the concealment and hiding that is in every exile
[for every exile is analogous to the exile of Egypt,
and as it is written regarding the exile of Egypt,
"And they did not listen to Moshe because of shortness of spirit and hard labor,"
so too is it in every exile,
that there are many trials in the observance of Torah and mitzvos],
then
(at the time of Haman's decree)
the concealment and hiding was even greater,
and nevertheless,
at the time of the Giving of the Torah,
when Israel were at the peak of elevation,
there was only the beginning
("they began to do"),
and at the time of Haman's decree,
when they were at the peak of lowliness,
specifically then they received what they had begun at the Giving of the Torah.
And he explains this,
that at the time of the decree,
their observance of Torah and mitzvos was with self-sacrifice (mesirus nefesh).
[In addition to the fact that they had self-sacrifice not to deny G-d, heaven forbid,
[as explained in Torah Ohr,
that if they had converted they would not have been harmed,
for the decree was only against the Jews,
and nevertheless no foreign thought entered their minds, heaven forbid],
they had self-sacrifice also for the observance of Torah and mitzvos,
to the extent that they assembled many congregations to study Torah with self-sacrifice.]
And the arousal of their self-sacrifice was through Mordechai the Jew,
the Moshe of his generation.
And this is "And the Jews received what they had begun to do,"
for at the Giving of the Torah there was only the beginning, and at the time of Haman's decree there was the receiving,
for through their having actual self-sacrifice for Torah and mitzvos at that time, they were elevated
(in this matter)
to a more sublime level than they were at the time of the Giving of the Torah,
and therefore specifically then there was the receiving,
"and the Jews received."

sections.sectionSummaryBrief: The explanation of "beaten for the light" could relate to reaching self-sacrifice through being crushed, but the context suggests it also connects to Moshe nourishing faith into inwardness.

translations.translation: And seemingly, one could say,
that the explanation of "beaten for the light,"
that through "beaten"
(broken and crushed)
one reaches the "light" (maor),
is an explanation of this, that specifically at the time of the decree they came to self-sacrifice in a most sublime manner.
For self-sacrifice is from the essence of the soul, which is beyond revelation,
the "light" (maor)
(from which the light emanates),
and through being in a state of "beaten"
(broken and crushed),
the essence of the soul was revealed,
the "light" (maor).
But from the flow and order of topics in the maamar, that the explanation of "beaten for the light" comes after the topic of "Raaya Meheimna,"
it implies
that the matter of "beaten for the light" also relates to this, that Moshe nourishes and sustains the faith so that it should be in inwardness.
